Chapter 3. Letting Go of Preconceptions and Expectations.
Think about this for a second—most of us carry around an invisible script. It’s full of beliefs about how things are supposed to go, how people should behave, and how life ought to unfold. These expectations shape every conversation, every moment, and honestly, they can set us up for disappointment when reality doesn’t quite match up to our inner story.
In Zen, there’s this gentle nudge to notice those scripts. To see how they box us in, and to practice letting them go, even just a little bit.
Imagine someone arriving at a meditation retreat, full of hope. Maybe they’re thinking, “After a few days of silence and practice, all my problems will just melt away.” But what happens? The old habits and anxieties creep back in. The mind resists, the body aches, and suddenly, frustration shows up. It’s so easy to blame the practice, the teacher, or even ourselves. But underneath all that, something more subtle is at work—a slow unraveling of that need for things to be different.
Letting go of preconceptions isn’t about giving up or tuning out. It’s about realizing that when we cling to fixed ideas—about ourselves, about others, about the world—it actually creates suffering. If our minds are jam-packed with judgments and expectations, there’s hardly any room for something new to come in. But if we’re willing to let go, even just for a moment, a little freedom sneaks in.
Now, I won’t pretend it’s always comfortable. There’s a real vulnerability in meeting life without the shield of certainty. But there’s also a quiet strength that comes with it. Without all those rigid expectations, suddenly, we’re able to respond to what’s actually happening—with genuine creativity and openness.
Picture a conversation that could’ve turned into an argument, but instead, it becomes an opportunity for understanding. Or maybe a setback at work—what if it wasn’t a failure, but a chance to learn, instead of a reason for self-criticism?
There’s a story about someone who spent years trying to be the perfect meditator. They thought discipline or skill was the answer, but eventually, they realized the real obstacle was the belief that things should be different. The moment they saw that belief for what it was—a thought, not a fact—something shifted. Suddenly, practice wasn’t about “achieving” a certain state. It was about being present with whatever showed up, pleasant or not.
And this attitude? It goes way beyond meditation. In relationships, it means listening without assuming you already know. Letting yourself be surprised. Allowing others to grow and change. At work, it means tackling each task with curiosity, instead of just going through the motions. And when life gets tough, it’s about meeting pain or disappointment with compassion, not resistance.
Over time, you start to see—the real freedom isn’t in controlling everything around you. It’s in letting go of the need for life to stick to your personal script. Suddenly, all that unpredictability doesn’t feel so threatening. In fact, life becomes more vivid, more alive. Each moment, when it’s not weighed down by expectations, has its own quiet beauty to reveal.
